Julian,

Thanks again for the productive discovery call earlier this week. As discussed, we're ready to hand off implementation to your engineering team and wanted to share a pragmatic runbook that covers SDK setup, endpoint migration, retries/timeouts, and rate-limit handling so your mobile engineers can get started configuring the client.

Attached: redwood-sdk-setup-quickstart.pdf (quick start), acme-integration-checklist.xlsx (mutual action items), timeout-retry-guidelines.md (recommended defaults). I also dropped a copy of the runbook in the shared Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1AbCdEfG-acme-onboarding

Short proposed plan (high level):
- Week 0: Access & creds — confirm service account, environment keys, and staging VPC access.
- Week 1: SDK install + local smoke tests (Android + iOS) using our test model endpoint.
- Week 2: Gradual endpoint migration (canary 5% -> 25% -> 100%) with monitoring hooks.
- Week 3: Load test + production cutover + post-cutover validation.

Key owners we suggest:
- Acme: Julian (eng lead) — primary contact for canary rollouts + QA.
- Redwood: Marissa — SDK support and integration troubleshooting; Grace — program PM for scheduling and checklist tracking.

Ask for you: please confirm the primary engineer who will be in the thread, and whether you prefer rolling migration by client version or by percentage traffic at the gateway. Also call out any internal SLOs you want us to target for latency and error budgets.

I put a few implementation notes inline in the attached checklist. If it's helpful we can schedule a 30-minute handoff next week to walk through the sample code and the retry strategy.

A few implementation questions the team flagged that we'd like guidance on before the handoff call:

2) Retries & backoff: recommended retry counts and exponential backoff parameters for mobile clients with intermittent connectivity.

Julian — looping in answers here and dropping brief sample snippets. Happy to expand during the call.

1) Endpoint migration
- We support header-based routing (set X-Redwood-Model: model-name) which allows you to keep the same base URL and swap model variants by header. If you want zero-client-change, we can provision a DNS/Proxy toggle for you, but header toggle is simplest for client-side.
- Rollout recommendation: canary by percentage at the gateway (5/25/100) + client-side version pinning for the first two waves. That gives you control to rollback by routing rather than forcing an app update.

2) Retries & backoff (mobile recommendations)
- Retry policy: idempotent requests only (e.g., embeddings, non-stateful generate calls) — default retry attempts: 2 (in addition to original), with exponential backoff base 500ms, multiplier 2.0, max backoff 8s.
- For generate/chat where partial outputs may be produced, prefer client de-dup token or server-side request-id to detect duplicates rather than blind retries.

3) Timeouts
- Connect timeout: 3s
- Socket/read timeout: 10s for short requests; for streaming generation allow up to 60s with keep-alives.
- Background uploads (batching): you can allow longer timeouts (30s) but use robust retry and a persisted queue on failure.

4) Rate limiting
- Client-side: implement a leaky/bucket token limiter. For mobile, we recommend a conservative baseline: 5 RPS per active client instance during foreground interaction, with burst allowance of 20 requests.
- Server-side: Redwood returns 429 with Retry-After in seconds when throttled. Honor Retry-After and back off. For background jobs, add jitter to reduce thundering herd.

5) Sample snippets (minimal)
- Android (Kotlin) — retry wrapper pseudocode:
  class RetryClient(private val base: OkHttpClient) {
    suspend fun call(req: Request): Response {
      var attempt = 0
      var backoff = 500L
      while (true) {
        try {
          val resp = base.newCall(req).execute()
          if (!shouldRetry(resp)) return resp
        } catch (e: IOException) {
          // network error — continue to retry
        }
        if (++attempt > 2) throw IOException("max retries")
        delay(backoff + jitter())
        backoff = min(8000L, backoff * 2)
      }
    }
  }

- iOS (Swift) — token refresh + simple retry outline:
  func performRequest(_ request: URLRequest, attempts: Int = 0, completion: @escaping (Result<Data, Error>) -> Void) {
    let task = session.dataTask(with: request) { data, resp, err in
      if let status = (resp as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode, status == 429, let retry = (resp as? HTTPURLResponse)?.allHeaderFields["Retry-After"] as? String, let seconds = Int(retry) {
        DispatchQueue.global().asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + .seconds(seconds)) {
          performRequest(request, attempts: attempts + 1, completion: completion)
        }
        return
      }
      // handle data / errors / retry on network errors similarly
    }
    task.resume()
  }

Implementation notes and traps
- Use server-issued short-lived tokens (we support 1–24h TTLs). Refresh proactively (on 401) to avoid mid-request failures.
- For streaming, ensure socket keep-alive and handle partial transcripts (resume via request-id where applicable).
- Observability: instrument per-call latency, tokens consumed, 429 counts; plug these into a canary dashboard during rollout.

Attachments in Drive include the quickstart and a longer developer guide with full code samples: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1AbCdEfG-acme-onboarding
